# Water turbine (`water_turbine`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/energy.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Energy & engines (`energy`)
- Deps: needs water_wheel; helped by calculus, machine_tools, dynamo_electric_motor
- Core idea: A water turbine extracts energy as water changes speed or direction in its runner. In a reaction turbine the runner passages stay full. Fixed guide vanes swirl the water into curved runner blades all round the wheel at once; the blades are shaped so that the water enters without shock and leaves with almost no speed left, which gives 80 to 90 % efficiency. A reaction runner works under water, is not limited to falls the size of its own diameter, and uses any head from 1 m to hundreds of metres fed through a pressure pipe. For very high heads a jet from a nozzle hits split cup-shaped buckets that turn the water back through nearly 180 degrees (Pelton wheel). These buckets run in air.
- Pitfalls:
  - Flat paddles in a casing; without curved blades and guide vanes it is only a bad water wheel
  - Closing the valve of a long pressure pipe quickly; the water hammer bursts the pipe
  - Running a reaction turbine partly empty or sucking air
  - Bucket speed equal to jet speed on a Pelton wheel; it should be about half
- History: islamic: 9th–12th c. – horizontal wheels fed by a jet from a tall drop tower (aruba penstock) common in the Near East and Iran; europe: 1750 – Segner's reaction wheel, analysed by Euler 1750–54; 1767 Borda's theory; 1822 Burdin coins the word turbine; 1827 Fourneyron's first working outward-flow turbine (about 6 hp, 80 % efficient); 1913 Kaplan's adjustable propeller turbine; americas: 1849 – Francis inward-flow turbine at Lowell, Massachusetts; 1880 Pelton's patent for the split-bucket wheel in California
- Read:
  - Terry S. Reynolds, Stronger than a Hundred Men: A History of the Vertical Water Wheel (1983)
  - Edwin T. Layton Jr., Scientific Technology, 1845–1900: The Hydraulic Turbine and the Origins of American Industrial Research, Technology and Culture 20 (1979)
